segments.t: On the motorway toward Valladolid, Paquita startles Macarena by mentioning the two shots she drank earlier, puts music on the car radio, and jokes about wearing her navy suit like a uniform. Together they laugh about the night Macarena walked onstage at the Goya Awards with her dress unzipped and Paquita chased after her on live television. Listen to the Spanish first.
Ya está, ya estamos en el coche.
¿Qué va a pasar? No pasa nada.
Me he tomado dos chupitos porque iba a la boda.
Iba a conducir Magüi.
Ten cuidado.
Mira, te pongo música. ¿Qué te pongo?
Me da igual, lo que quieras.
Estás muy guapa.
Este traje lo conoces de memoria. Lo tengo de uniforme.
Ya sabes que soy muy clásica. La que está muy guapa eres tú.
¿Te acuerdas de la primera vez que fui a los Goya?
Cinco minutos antes me quise cambiar de vestido.
Saliste con la cremallera bajada.
Saliste detrás de mí delante de toda España.
Mis cinco minutos de fama.
Let's go through their conversation on the road.
Ya está, ya estamos en el coche.
'There we go, we're in the car now.' Literally already it is, a brisk two-word phrase meaning all sorted, done, or there we go, followed by already we are in the car.
¿Qué va a pasar? No pasa nada.
'What's going to happen? Nothing's wrong.' Literally nothing happens, one of Spain's most reassuring everyday sentences for it's fine or nothing is wrong.
Me he tomado dos chupitos porque iba a la boda.
'I had two shots because I was going to the wedding.' For food and drinks, Spanish prefers take over have, adding the little word for myself to sound casual and complete.
Iba a conducir Magüi.
'Magüi was going to drive.' Putting Magüi at the end of was going to drive highlights who the designated driver was meant to be.
Ten cuidado.
'Be careful.' Literally have care: the short one-syllable command form of have pairs with care to warn a driver or friend.
Mira, te pongo música. ¿Qué te pongo?
'Look, I'll put some music on for you. What shall I put on?' Where English says I'll put on, Spanish uses simple present I put for an immediate offer, and repeats it in what do I put for you.
Me da igual, lo que quieras.
'I don't mind, whatever you like.' Adding the tiny word for to me in front of gives equal turns never mind into I don't mind, followed by literally that which you want.
Estás muy guapa.
'You look very pretty.' Using the temporary state form rather than permanent are turns pretty into you look very pretty today.
Este traje lo conoces de memoria. Lo tengo de uniforme.
'You know this suit by heart. It's like my uniform.' Naming this suit first lets Paquita echo it with masculine it before you know, and of memory is the Spanish idiom for by heart.
Ya sabes que soy muy clásica. La que está muy guapa eres tú.

'You know I'm very classic. You're the one who looks very pretty.' Look at how the two words for know contrast across these lines: earlier know meant being familiar with a suit, while here you know introduces a fact. Then the feminine one who looks very pretty is you.
¿Te acuerdas de la primera vez que fui a los Goya?
'Do you remember the first time I went to the Goyas?' For an occasion or an instance rather than clock time, Spanish uses a short feminine word, so first takes its feminine ending.
Cinco minutos antes me quise cambiar de vestido.
'Five minutes beforehand I wanted to change my dress.' Completed past I wanted means tried or decided on the spot, and changing outfits literally says change of dress rather than change my dress.
Saliste con la cremallera bajada.
'You went out onstage with your zip down.' Feminine zip is followed by lowered with a matching feminine ending, and Spanish says the zip rather than your zip.
Saliste detrás de mí delante de toda España.
'You came out right behind me in front of all Spain.' Notice the two contrasting location phrases in one breath: literally behind of me and in front of all Spain.
Mis cinco minutos de fama.
'My five minutes of fame.' Because five minutes is plural, my adds a final s to match, unlike singular my in earlier lines. Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Ya está, ya estamos en el coche.
¿Qué va a pasar? No pasa nada.
Me he tomado dos chupitos porque iba a la boda.
Iba a conducir Magüi.
Ten cuidado.
Mira, te pongo música. ¿Qué te pongo?
Me da igual, lo que quieras.
Estás muy guapa.
Este traje lo conoces de memoria. Lo tengo de uniforme.
Ya sabes que soy muy clásica. La que está muy guapa eres tú.
¿Te acuerdas de la primera vez que fui a los Goya?
Cinco minutos antes me quise cambiar de vestido.
Saliste con la cremallera bajada.
Saliste detrás de mí delante de toda España.
Mis cinco minutos de fama.
You heard 'tener cuidado' for 'be careful', 'de memoria' for 'by heart', and 'delante de' versus 'detrás de' for 'in front of' and 'behind'. See you in the next scene.
¡Buenas noches!
